Stiff Limb Syndrome: A Case Report and Diagnostic Criteria*
1,
2, 3
Sana Syed

1Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA 02116 USA
2Boston Medical Center, Boston, MA 02116 USA
2Harvard School of Public Health, Boston, MA 02115 USA

Case Description
65 year old female presented with
18 months of worsening lower
extremity
spasms,
which
predominantly
involved
the
thighs and caused her to rely on
crutches and a walker to
ambulate. These spasms were
precipitated by touch, stress and
voluntary activity. She also had
associated weight loss and a very
anxious demeanor.

She had an extensive workup and
responded well to a trial of
valium. However she was readmitted
3 times over the next 4 months for the
same symptoms and had additional
testing done. Abnormalities included
increased rheumatoid factor at 46,
mildly elevated CPK 364 and CRP
5. 7.
Other tests were negative
including HIV antibody, lyme titer, antiGAD antibodies and a heavy metal
screen. Her CSF studies were also
negative for oligoclonal bands, myelin
basic protein and VDRL. Her MRI
brain was unremarkable and MRI
cervical and lumbar spine did not
show any cord compression. She had
an EMG that revealed continuously
firing motor unit action potentials in
the lower extremities that were not
readily inhibited by the activation of
the antagonistic muscles. The needle
EMG examination showed findings
consistent with stiff person syndrome.

Results
The protracted course of her disease
is testament that there are no clear
guidelines for diagnosis of Stiff Limb
Syndrome. The initial concern was
for HTLV-1 versus primary lateral
sclerosis
versus
cervical
myelopathy, however stiff limb
syndrome was the diagnosis by
exclusion. On review of prior and
this current case, the diagnostic
criteria can be based on features of
increased tone mostly in lower
extremities (proximal or distal) with
sparing of axial muscles and good
response
to
valium,
with
characteristic
EMG
findings.

stiff limb syndrome still delays
diagnosis
and
accurate
management.

On exam she had increased tone
in her lower extremities, proximal
more than distal, but intact
strength and retained reflexes in
upper extremities but she was
unable to relax the lower
extremities.
She
had
hyperesthesia most notable over
the soles of her feet.

The patient however had focal
symptoms involving mainly the lower
extremities
without
truncal
or
upper

She was
treated with gabapentin, oxycontin,
valium and baclofen. However her
disease still progressed despite
polypharmacy, physical therapy and 3

rounds of IVIG.
